Quantum Entropy Contraction and Factorization from Hypercontractivity

LI GAO AND LIJUN WANG
Abstract.

We prove that hypercontractivity implies entropy contraction for a single quantum channel without assuming detailed balance. For primitive quantum Markov semigroups that are KMS-symmetric with respect to a faithful invariant state σ\sigma, we obtain the modified logarithmic Sobolev bound α1≥λ(2+log⁡‖σ−1‖∞)\alpha_{1}\geq\frac{\lambda}{(2+\log\|\sigma^{-1}\|_{\infty})}, where λ\lambda is the spectral gap. This removes the assumption of LpL_{p}-regularity previously needed to obtain this bound by comparison with the logarithmic Sobolev constant. As an application, we show that hypercontractivity of the average of two conditional expectations implies approximate tensorization of relative entropy.

1. Introduction

Quantitative convergence to equilibrium can be studied through either norm estimates or entropy inequalities. Hypercontractivity describes the improvement of weighted LpL_{p} norms under a Markov evolution, while entropy contraction measures the decrease of relative entropy. In this work, we study how hypercontractive estimates imply entropy contraction in finite-dimensional quantum systems. We note that the passage from hypercontractivity (HC) to entropy contraction (EC) already makes sense for a single channel. This is inspired by the work of Salez [20] in the classical setting, where neither reversibility nor regularity is assumed. In the quantum setting, the corresponding statement follows from Hirche–Rouzé–França [12, Proposition 5.4] through KMS duality. We combine it with a centering criterion that removes the multiplicative defect in a hyperbounded (HB) estimate using strict L2L_{2}-contraction on centered elements.

Let σ\sigma be a faithful state, and let Eσ​(X)=Tr⁡(σ​X)​IE_{\sigma}(X)=\Tr(\sigma X)I be the replacer map. The symmetric weighted norms are given by ‖X‖p,σ=‖σ1/(2​p)​X​σ1/(2​p)‖p\|X\|_{p,\sigma}=\|\sigma^{1/(2p)}X\sigma^{1/(2p)}\|_{p}, and D(ρ||σ)=Tr(ρlogρ−ρlogσ)D(\rho||\sigma)=\Tr(\rho\log\rho-\rho\log\sigma) denotes the quantum relative entropy. We write Φ∗\Phi_{*} for the trace dual of a Heisenberg-picture channel Φ\Phi.

Theorem A (Single-channel contraction).

Let Φ\Phi be a unital completely positive map preserving σ\sigma.

  1. (i)

    If 1<p<q<∞1<p<q<\infty and ‖Φ‖p→q,σ≤1\|\Phi\|_{p\to q,\sigma}\leq 1, then, for every state ρ\rho,

    D(Φ∗ρ∥σ)≤pqD(ρ∥σ).D(\Phi_{*}\rho\|\sigma)\leq\frac{p}{q}D(\rho\|\sigma).
  2. (ii)

    ‖Φ‖2→q,σ≤Mq,‖Φ−Eσ‖2→2,σ≤r,\|\Phi\|_{2\to q,\sigma}\leq M_{q},\qquad\|\Phi-E_{\sigma}\|_{2\to 2,\sigma}\leq r,

    where

    p=2+2​(q−2)​log⁡(1/r)q−2+q​log⁡(Mq/r)>2.p=2+\frac{2(q-2)\log(1/r)}{q-2+q\log(M_{q}/r)}>2.

Part (i) is established in Proposition 2.2 by applying [12, Proposition 5.4] and identifying the relevant KMS adjoint with the trace adjoint of the Petz map. Part (ii), proved in Theorem 2.4, is a weighted version of the centering method of Wang [25, Theorem 1.6]. In finite dimensions, a finite HB bound is automatic; its quantitative value determines the HC exponent supplied by the centering method. These statements require neither symmetry nor a semigroup structure and provide the direct norm-to-entropy passage used below.

For a primitive quantum Markov semigroup (QMS) Pt=e−t​ℒP_{t}=e^{-t\mathcal{L}}, we write α1\alpha_{1}, α2\alpha_{2}, and αH\alpha_{H} for the constants associated with the modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality (MLSI), the L2L_{2}-logarithmic Sobolev inequality (LSI), and HC, respectively; see Section 3.1 for detailed definitions. In the continuous-time setting, we obtain the following entropy contraction bounds.

Theorem B (MLSI from hyperboundedness).

Let (Pt)(P_{t}) be a finite-dimensional primitive KMS-symmetric QMS with a faithful invariant state σ\sigma and spectral gap λ>0\lambda>0. If, for some 2<q≤∞,tq>0,Mq≥12<q\leq\infty,\ t_{q}>0,\ M_{q}\geq 1,

‖Ptq‖2→q,σ≤Mq,\|P_{t_{q}}\|_{2\to q,\sigma}\leq M_{q},

α1≥β,α2≥2​β,αH≥β,β=(1−2/q)​λ2​[λ​tq+log⁡Mq+1−2/q].\alpha_{1}\geq\beta,\qquad\alpha_{2}\geq 2\beta,\qquad\alpha_{H}\geq\beta,\qquad\beta=\frac{(1-2/q)\lambda}{2[\lambda t_{q}+\log M_{q}+1-2/q]}.

Moreover, for a primitive QMS with positive KMS coercivity constant λKMS>0\lambda_{\mathrm{KMS}}>0, without assuming symmetry,

(1.1) α1≥αH2≥λKMS2+log⁡‖σ−1‖∞.\alpha_{1}\geq\frac{\alpha_{H}}{2}\geq\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{KMS}}}{2+\log\|\sigma^{-1}\|_{\infty}}.

We emphasize that no LpL_{p}-regularity is assumed in Theorem 3.3. This estimate is proved by constructing a local HC curve for small tt from the endpoint estimate and the spectral gap. Its slope at t=0t=0 gives the MLSI and LSI bounds; extending the curve to all times gives the HC bound. The interpolation method, the existence of an all-time HC curve, and the implication from HC to LSI without LpL_{p}-regularity are already present in [22]. Here the centering criterion in Lemma 2.3 provides explicit constants, and the HC-to-EC implication gives MLSI directly. The quantitative comparison with [22] is given in Section 3.2.

For KMS-symmetric semigroups, bounds similar to (1.1) were obtained for the LSI constant α2\alpha_{2}, but the comparison with the MLSI constant has required LpL_{p}-regularity. Here, we remove this technical assumption and obtain the bound for all KMS-symmetric semigroups. Related qualitative MLSI results for primitive KMS-symmetric semigroups also recently appeared in [27, 28].

Φav=E1+E22.\Phi_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{E_{1}+E_{2}}{2}.

Approximate tensorization (AT) means that there is a constant c>0c>0 such that

D(ρ||E𝒩∗ρ)≤c(D(ρ∥E1∗ρ)+D(ρ∥E2∗ρ))D(\rho||E_{\mathcal{N}*}\rho)\leq c\left(D(\rho\|E_{1*}\rho)+D(\rho\|E_{2*}\rho)\right)

for all states ρ\rho. When 𝒩≠ℳ\mathcal{N}\neq\mathcal{M}, AT with constant c>0c>0 implies EC for Φav,∗\Phi_{\mathrm{av},*} with coefficient 1−1/(2​c)1-1/(2c), by the chain rule and convexity [4, 8]. Our third theorem proves a converse whose AT constant depends only on the averaged EC coefficient.

Theorem C (AT from averaged EC).

Let Ei:ℳ→𝒩iE_{i}:\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{N}_{i}, i=1,2i=1,2, be conditional expectations preserving a common faithful state σ\sigma, and let E𝒩E_{\mathcal{N}} be the corresponding expectation onto 𝒩=𝒩1∩𝒩2\mathcal{N}=\mathcal{N}_{1}\cap\mathcal{N}_{2}. If, for some 0≤η<10\leq\eta<1 and every state ρ\rho,

D(E1∗ρ+E2∗ρ2∥E𝒩∗ρ)≤ηD(ρ||E𝒩∗ρ),D(\frac{E_{1*}\rho+E_{2*}\rho}{2}\|E_{\mathcal{N}*}\rho)\leq\eta D(\rho||E_{\mathcal{N}*}\rho),

then

(1.2) D(ρ||E𝒩∗ρ)≤32​(1−η)(D(ρ∥E1∗ρ)+D(ρ∥E2∗ρ)).D(\rho||E_{\mathcal{N}*}\rho)\leq\frac{3}{2(1-\eta)}\left(D(\rho\|E_{1*}\rho)+D(\rho\|E_{2*}\rho)\right).

This theorem makes averaged EC and AT quantitatively equivalent up to universal constants. The proof uses the quantum Jensen–Shannon divergence and the triangle inequality for the square root of this divergence [24]. Approximate tensorization for noncommuting conditional expectations and its complete versions were studied in [4, 11]. Gao and Rouzé [11, Corollary 5.4 and Remark 5.5] also obtain index-independent bounds from mixing in completely positive order, a condition of ultracontractive L1→L∞L_{1}\to L_{\infty} type; an index factor enters when one converts L2L_{2} estimates into that mixing condition. Our result starts with an entropy contraction estimate and converts it to AT without an additional index factor. As an application of Theorem A, when 𝒩=ℂ​I\mathcal{N}=\mathbb{C}I, the hypercontractivity of the average channel ρ↦12(E1∗ρ+E2∗ρ)\rho\mapsto\frac{1}{2}(E_{1*}\rho+E_{2*}\rho) supplies the EC hypothesis needed to obtain AT.

Section 2 develops the single-channel estimates. Section 3 treats quantum Markov semigroups and discusses entropy decay from time zero as well as delayed estimates. Section 4 proves the implication from averaged EC to AT.

2. Entropy contraction via hypercontractivity

We derive entropy contraction from hypercontractivity using a dual form of [12, Proposition 5.4]. Hypercontractivity can be obtained from a hyperbounded endpoint and strict L2L_{2} contraction on centered observables, using a weighted version of the method in [25, Theorem 1.6]. The centered criterion will be used directly for semigroups in Section 3.

2.1. Weighted norms and state-preserving channels

Throughout the paper, let B⁡(ℋ)B(\mathcal{H}) denote the algebra of linear operators on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} and let Tr\Tr denote the standard matrix trace. We identify states with density matrices and fix a faithful state σ>0\sigma>0, Tr⁡σ=1\Tr\sigma=1. All logarithms are natural.

For 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty, recall the symmetric weighted noncommutative LpL_{p} norms of [14, equations (10)–(12)], defined by

(2.1) ‖X‖p,σ=‖σ1/(2​p)​X​σ1/(2​p)‖p,‖X‖∞,σ=‖X‖∞,\|X\|_{p,\sigma}=\bigl\|\sigma^{1/(2p)}X\sigma^{1/(2p)}\bigr\|_{p},\qquad\|X\|_{\infty,\sigma}=\|X\|_{\infty},

where the pp-norm on the right is the Schatten pp-norm. We write Lp​(σ)L_{p}(\sigma) for this normed space, and ‖T‖p→q,σ\|T\|_{p\to q,\sigma} for the induced operator norm; the subscript σ\sigma is omitted whenever there is no ambiguity. For p=2p=2, L2​(σ)L_{2}(\sigma) is a Hilbert space equipped with the Kubo–Martin–Schwinger (KMS) inner product

(2.2) ⟨X,Y⟩σ=Tr⁡(X∗​σ1/2​Y​σ1/2),Γσ​(X)=σ1/2​X​σ1/2,\langle X,Y\rangle_{\sigma}=\Tr(X^{*}\sigma^{1/2}Y\sigma^{1/2}),\qquad\Gamma_{\sigma}(X)=\sigma^{1/2}X\sigma^{1/2},

where Γσ\Gamma_{\sigma} is the weighting map. For real ss we write Γσs​(X)=σs/2​X​σs/2\Gamma_{\sigma}^{s}(X)=\sigma^{s/2}X\sigma^{s/2}. For conjugate exponents 1/p+1/p′=11/p+1/p^{\prime}=1, weighted Hölder duality gives

(2.3) |⟨X,Y⟩σ|≤‖X‖p,σ​‖Y‖p′,σ,‖X‖p,σ=sup‖Y‖p′,σ≤1|⟨Y,X⟩σ|.|\langle X,Y\rangle_{\sigma}|\leq\|X\|_{p,\sigma}\|Y\|_{p^{\prime},\sigma},\qquad\|X\|_{p,\sigma}=\sup_{\|Y\|_{p^{\prime},\sigma}\leq 1}|\langle Y,X\rangle_{\sigma}|.

The norms are monotone: ‖X‖p,σ≤‖X‖q,σ\|X\|_{p,\sigma}\leq\|X\|_{q,\sigma} for p≤qp\leq q. The spaces Lp​(σ)L_{p}(\sigma) form a complex interpolation scale [5, Theorem 4],

(2.4) ‖T‖pθ→qθ≤‖T‖p0→q01−θ​‖T‖p1→q1θ,1pθ=1−θp0+θp1,1qθ=1−θq0+θq1.\|T\|_{p_{\theta}\to q_{\theta}}\leq\|T\|_{p_{0}\to q_{0}}^{1-\theta}\|T\|_{p_{1}\to q_{1}}^{\theta},\quad\frac{1}{p_{\theta}}=\frac{1-\theta}{p_{0}}+\frac{\theta}{p_{1}},\quad\frac{1}{q_{\theta}}=\frac{1-\theta}{q_{0}}+\frac{\theta}{q_{1}}.

We will also use the analytic-family version of Riesz–Thorin interpolation in Section 3.

A quantum channel in the Heisenberg picture is a unital completely positive map Φ:B⁡(ℋ)→B⁡(ℋ)\Phi:B(\mathcal{H})\to B(\mathcal{H}). Its trace dual Φ∗\Phi_{*} in the Schrödinger picture is a completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) map given by

Tr⁡(Φ∗​ρ​X)=Tr⁡(ρ​Φ​X).\Tr(\Phi_{*}\rho\,X)=\Tr(\rho\,\Phi X).

Throughout the paper, we assume that Φ\Phi is σ\sigma-preserving, i.e. σ=Φ∗​σ\sigma=\Phi_{*}\sigma is an invariant state. Every σ\sigma-preserving channel is contractive

‖Φ⁡(X)‖p,σ≤‖X‖p,σ\|\Phi(X)\|_{p,\sigma}\leq\|X\|_{p,\sigma}

on Lp​(σ)L_{p}(\sigma) for 1≤p≤∞1\leq p\leq\infty. The KMS adjoint with respect to L2​(σ)L_{2}(\sigma) is

(2.5) Φ#=Γσ−1​Φ∗​Γσ.\Phi^{\#}=\Gamma_{\sigma}^{-1}\Phi_{*}\Gamma_{\sigma}.

This is exactly the Petz recovery map of Φ∗\Phi_{*} with respect to the invariant state σ\sigma in the Heisenberg picture. In particular, Φ#\Phi^{\#} is unital and completely positive and satisfies σ∘Φ#=σ\sigma\circ\Phi^{\#}=\sigma. We call Φ\Phi KMS-symmetric if Φ#=Φ\Phi^{\#}=\Phi.

2.2. From norm estimates to entropy contraction

For two states ρ,ω\rho,\omega, their Umegaki relative entropy [23] is

D(ρ∥ω)=Trρ(logρ−logω)D(\rho\|\omega)=\Tr\rho(\log\rho-\log\omega)

if supp⁡ρ⊆supp⁡ω\supp\rho\subseteq\supp\omega, and is +∞+\infty otherwise. We recall three functional inequalities for state-preserving quantum channels.

Definition 2.1 (Hypercontractivity, hyperboundedness and entropy contraction).

Let Φ:B⁡(ℋ)→B⁡(ℋ)\Phi:B(\mathcal{H})\to B(\mathcal{H}) be a unital completely positive map and assume Φ\Phi preserves a fixed faithful state σ=Φ∗​σ\sigma=\Phi_{*}\sigma. For 1<p<q<∞1<p<q<\infty, we say that

  1. i)

    Φ\Phi is hypercontractive (HC) at (p,q)(p,q) if

    ‖Φ‖p→q,σ≤1.\|\Phi\|_{p\to q,\sigma}\leq 1.
  2. ii)

    Φ\Phi is hyperbounded (HB) at (p,q)(p,q) if for some 1≤M<∞1\leq M<\infty,

    ‖Φ‖p→q,σ≤M.\|\Phi\|_{p\to q,\sigma}\leq M.
  3. iii)

    Φ\Phi satisfies (relative) entropy contraction with respect to σ\sigma if for some 0<η<10<\eta<1,

    (2.6) D(Φ∗ρ∥σ)≤ηD(ρ∥σ),∀ state ρ.\displaystyle D(\Phi_{*}\rho\|\sigma)\leq\eta D(\rho\|\sigma),\qquad\forall\ \text{ state }\rho.

In finite dimensions, a hyperbounded estimate always holds and the information lies in the value of MM and the dependence on the parameters (p,q)(p,q). Hypercontractivity is the case M=1M=1, which can hold only if Φ\Phi is primitive, i.e. Φk\Phi^{k} converges to EσE_{\sigma}. In particular, σ\sigma is the unique invariant state and the fixed-point space 𝒩:={X|Φ⁡(X)=X}=ℂ​1\mathcal{N}:=\{X\ |\ \Phi(X)=X\}=\mathbb{C}1 is trivial. By the data processing inequality, the relative entropy is always monotone non-increasing

D(Φ∗ρ∥σ)≤D(ρ∥σ).D(\Phi_{*}\rho\|\sigma)\leq D(\rho\|\sigma)\ .

The entropy contraction (2.6) asserts a uniform contraction factor strictly smaller than one and is also called a strong data processing inequality (SDPI).

Since Φ∗​σ=σ\Phi_{*}\sigma=\sigma, the Petz map of Φ∗\Phi_{*} at σ\sigma satisfies

(2.7) Rσ,Φ∗=Γσ​Φ​Γσ−1,Rσ,Φ∗∗=Γσ−1​Φ∗​Γσ=Φ#.R_{\sigma,\Phi_{*}}=\Gamma_{\sigma}\Phi\Gamma_{\sigma}^{-1},\qquad R_{\sigma,\Phi_{*}}^{*}=\Gamma_{\sigma}^{-1}\Phi_{*}\Gamma_{\sigma}=\Phi^{\#}.

Here ∗* denotes the trace adjoint. Weighted Hölder duality (2.3) gives

(2.8) ‖Φ‖p→q,σ=‖Φ#‖q′→p′,σ,‖Φ#‖1→1,σ=1.\|\Phi\|_{p\to q,\sigma}=\|\Phi^{\#}\|_{q^{\prime}\to p^{\prime},\sigma},\qquad\|\Phi^{\#}\|_{1\to 1,\sigma}=1.

Applying [12, Proposition 5.4] using the KMS duality above, we obtain a quantum analogue of Salez’s result [20, Theorem 1] for classical Markov maps. No symmetry (reversibility) is required, as in the classical case [20].

Proposition 2.2 (Entropy contraction from hypercontractivity).

Let 1<p≤q<∞1<p\leq q<\infty. Suppose Φ\Phi is a σ\sigma-preserving channel satisfying

(2.9) ‖Φ‖p→q,σ≤1.\|\Phi\|_{p\to q,\sigma}\leq 1.

Then, for every state ρ\rho,

(2.10) D(Φ∗ρ∥σ)≤pqD(ρ∥σ).D(\Phi_{*}\rho\|\sigma)\leq\frac{p}{q}D(\rho\|\sigma).
Proof.

For 0≤t≤10\leq t\leq 1, set

at=(1−t/q)−1,bt=(1−t/p)−1.a_{t}=(1-t/q)^{-1},\qquad b_{t}=(1-t/p)^{-1}.

By (2.8) and (2.9), complex interpolation yields

‖Φ#‖at→bt,σ≤1.\|\Phi^{\#}\|_{a_{t}\to b_{t},\sigma}\leq 1.

For a faithful state ρ\rho, take X=Γσ−1​ρX=\Gamma_{\sigma}^{-1}\rho. Then Φ#​X=Γσ−1​Φ∗​ρ\Phi^{\#}X=\Gamma_{\sigma}^{-1}\Phi_{*}\rho, and both have unit weighted L1L_{1} norm. The norm–entropy derivative [12, Lemma 5.1] is

dd​slog∥Γσ−1ρ∥s,σ|s=1=D(ρ∥σ).\left.\frac{d}{ds}\log\|\Gamma_{\sigma}^{-1}\rho\|_{s,\sigma}\right|_{s=1}=D(\rho\|\sigma).

Taking logarithms and differentiating the interpolated estimate at t=0t=0 gives

1pD(Φ∗ρ∥σ)≤1qD(ρ∥σ),\frac{1}{p}D(\Phi_{*}\rho\|\sigma)\leq\frac{1}{q}D(\rho\|\sigma),

which is (2.10). The result for a general state ρ\rho follows by approximating it with the faithful states (1−ε)​ρ+ε​σ(1-\varepsilon)\rho+\varepsilon\sigma. ∎

Hypercontractivity also implies primitivity. Recall that a channel is primitive if its iterates Φk\Phi^{k} converge to the scalar expectation Eσ​(X)=Tr⁡(σ​X)​IE_{\sigma}(X)=\Tr(\sigma X)I. If ‖Φ‖p→q,σ≤1\|\Phi\|_{p\to q,\sigma}\leq 1 with p<qp<q, iteration gives

(2.11) D(Φ∗kρ∥σ)≤(pq)kD(ρ∥σ)→0, as k→∞.D(\Phi_{*}^{k}\rho\|\sigma)\leq\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)^{k}D(\rho\|\sigma)\to 0,\qquad\text{ as }k\to\infty.

By quantum Pinsker’s inequality [14, Section I], this yields trace norm convergence

∥Φ∗kρ−σ∥12≤2(pq)kD(ρ∥σ).\|\Phi_{*}^{k}\rho-\sigma\|_{1}^{2}\leq 2\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)^{k}D(\rho\|\sigma).

When the fixed-point algebra 𝒩\mathcal{N} is nontrivial, relative hyperboundedness was introduced in [3] using amalgamated norms relative to 𝒩\mathcal{N}. If EE is the fixed-point conditional expectation and Φ​E=E​Φ=E\Phi E=E\Phi=E, the corresponding entropy contraction is formulated using D(ρ∥E∗ρ)D(\rho\|E_{*}\rho), the decoherence-free relative entropy introduced in [2, Definition 3.3], whose reference state E∗​ρE_{*}\rho depends on the input ρ\rho. However, for the amalgamated-norm formulation of [3], a nontrivially decohering QMS on B⁡(ℋ)B(\mathcal{H}) cannot satisfy a defect-free HC curve with positive initial slope when ℂ​I⊊𝒩⊊B⁡(ℋ)\mathbb{C}I\subsetneq\mathcal{N}\subsetneq B(\mathcal{H}); see [3, Theorems 2.4(i) and 5.1].

2.3. From hyperboundedness to hypercontractivity

It follows by an argument similar to that of Proposition 2.2 that hyperboundedness implies entropy contraction with a defect

∥Φ∥p→q,σ≤M⟹D(Φ∗ρ∥σ)≤pqD(ρ∥σ)+plogM.\|\Phi\|_{p\to q,\sigma}\leq M\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad D(\Phi_{*}\rho\|\sigma)\leq\frac{p}{q}D(\rho\|\sigma)+p\log M\ .

We now use strict L2L_{2} coercivity to remove the defect term. The key ingredient is an LpL_{p}-norm analogue of the Rothaus lemma, based on a centering argument. We state the centering argument separately, as it will be reused in Section 3.

Define the expectation map

(2.12) Eσ​(X)=Tr⁡(σ​X)​I.E_{\sigma}(X)=\Tr(\sigma X)I.

This gives the KMS orthogonal decomposition L2​(σ)=ℂ​I⊕ker⁡EσL_{2}(\sigma)=\mathbb{C}I\oplus\ker E_{\sigma}, with

‖a​I+X0‖2,σ2=|a|2+‖X0‖2,σ2\|aI+X_{0}\|_{2,\sigma}^{2}=|a|^{2}+\|X_{0}\|_{2,\sigma}^{2}

for X0∈ker⁡EσX_{0}\in\ker E_{\sigma}. Every σ\sigma-preserving channel satisfies Φ​Eσ=Eσ​Φ=Eσ\Phi E_{\sigma}=E_{\sigma}\Phi=E_{\sigma}, and therefore

(2.13) ‖Φ−Eσ‖2→2,σ=‖Φ|ker⁡Eσ‖2→2,σ.\|\Phi-E_{\sigma}\|_{2\to 2,\sigma}=\|\Phi|_{\ker E_{\sigma}}\|_{2\to 2,\sigma}.

Let Φ\Phi be a σ\sigma-preserving channel and 2≤p<∞2\leq p<\infty. If

Lemma 2.9 of [29], in its reversed form for p>2p>2, gives

(2.15) ‖X‖p,σ2≤|Tr⁡(σ​X)|2+(p−1)​‖X−Eσ​X‖p,σ2.\|X\|_{p,\sigma}^{2}\leq|\Tr(\sigma X)|^{2}+(p-1)\|X-E_{\sigma}X\|_{p,\sigma}^{2}.

Writing X=a​I+X0X=aI+X_{0}, with X0∈ker⁡EσX_{0}\in\ker E_{\sigma}, we obtain

‖Φ​X‖p,σ2≤|a|2+(p−1)​‖Φ​X0‖p,σ2≤|a|2+‖X0‖2,σ2=‖X‖2,σ2.∎\displaystyle\|\Phi X\|_{p,\sigma}^{2}\leq|a|^{2}+(p-1)\|\Phi X_{0}\|_{p,\sigma}^{2}\leq|a|^{2}+\|X_{0}\|_{2,\sigma}^{2}=\|X\|_{2,\sigma}^{2}.\qed

‖Φ​X‖p,σ≤‖Φ​X‖2,σ1−θp​‖Φ​X‖q,σθp≤r1−θp​Mqθp​‖X‖2,σ.\|\Phi X\|_{p,\sigma}\leq\|\Phi X\|_{2,\sigma}^{1-\theta_{p}}\|\Phi X\|_{q,\sigma}^{\theta_{p}}\leq r^{1-\theta_{p}}M_{q}^{\theta_{p}}\|X\|_{2,\sigma}.

Thus Lemma 2.3 gives hypercontractivity whenever

(2.21) (p−1)​r2​(1−θp)​Mq2​θp≤1.(p-1)r^{2(1-\theta_{p})}M_{q}^{2\theta_{p}}\leq 1.

By the inequalities log⁡(p−1)≤p−2\log(p-1)\leq p-2 and θp≤q⁡(p−2)/(2​(q−2))\theta_{p}\leq q(p-2)/(2(q-2)), the logarithm of the left-hand side is bounded by

log⁡((p−1)​r2​(1−θp)​Mq2​θp)≤2​log⁡r+(1+qq−2​log⁡(Mq/r))​(p−2)≤0,\log\left((p-1)r^{2(1-\theta_{p})}M_{q}^{2\theta_{p}}\right)\leq 2\log r+\left(1+\frac{q}{q-2}\log(M_{q}/r)\right)(p-2)\leq 0,

where pp is chosen as in (2.20) to ensure the last inequality. This proves hypercontractivity at (2,p)(2,p), which gives entropy contraction (2.19) by Proposition 2.2. ∎

Remark 2.5.

a) For a primitive channel Φ\Phi that is KMS-symmetric with respect to σ\sigma, condition ii) (2.17) is always satisfied. Indeed, under KMS symmetry, Φ\Phi is a self-adjoint operator on L2​(σ)L_{2}(\sigma) commuting with EσE_{\sigma}, and hence the norm of Φ−Eσ\Phi-E_{\sigma} equals its spectral radius, which is strictly less than 1 by primitivity.

b) The above qualitative implication from strict centered L2L_{2} contraction to a nontrivial HC exponent is known in the classical setting [1, Theorem 3(a), (c), p. 928]. In finite-dimensional noncommutative algebras with a tracial state, Wang [25, Theorem 1.6] proves the corresponding s→2s\to 2 characterization for 1<s<21<s<2. Our argument above is a weighted version in the dual range using the same pp-convexity inequality.

3. Quantum Markov semigroups

In this section, we discuss how a hypercontractive or hyperbounded estimate implies entropy contraction in continuous time.

3.1. Functional inequalities

A quantum Markov semigroup (QMS) is a continuous semigroup (Pt)t≥0:B⁡(ℋ)→B⁡(ℋ)(P_{t})_{t\geq 0}:B(\mathcal{H})\to B(\mathcal{H}) of unital completely positive maps satisfying Pt∘Ps=Pt+sP_{t}\circ P_{s}=P_{t+s} for s,t≥0s,t\geq 0 and P0=idP_{0}=\id. Throughout this section, we assume ℋ\mathcal{H} is finite-dimensional, and the semigroup is primitive with a faithful invariant state σ\sigma. We write Pt=e−t​ℒP_{t}=e^{-t\mathcal{L}} with the generator

ℒX=−limt→01t(PtX−X),\mathcal{L}X=-\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{1}{t}(P_{t}X-X)\ ,

and K=ker⁡EσK=\ker E_{\sigma}. KMS symmetry is assumed only where stated, and we omit σ\sigma from pp-norms when it is clear from the context. For a faithful state ρ\rho, the entropy production is [14, equations (5)–(6)]

(3.1) ℐℒ(ρ)=Tr[(ℒ∗ρ)(logρ−logσ)]=−dd​tD(Pt∗ρ∥σ)|t=0.\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{L}}(\rho)=\Tr[(\mathcal{L}_{*}\rho)(\log\rho-\log\sigma)]=-\left.\frac{d}{dt}D(P_{t*}\rho\|\sigma)\right|_{t=0}.

The HC constant αH\alpha_{H} is the supremum of α≥0\alpha\geq 0 such that

(3.2) ‖Pt‖2→1+e2​α​t,σ≤1(t≥0).\|P_{t}\|_{2\to 1+e^{2\alpha t},\sigma}\leq 1\qquad(t\geq 0).

For X>0X>0, write Y=Γσ12​(X)=σ14​X​σ14Y=\Gamma_{\sigma}^{\frac{1}{2}}(X)=\sigma^{\frac{1}{4}}X\sigma^{\frac{1}{4}}, and set

Ent2,σ(X)=12{Tr[Y2(logY2−logσ)]−Tr(Y2)logTr(Y2)},ℰ(X)=Re⟨X,ℒX⟩σ.\Ent_{2,\sigma}(X)=\frac{1}{2}\{\Tr[Y^{2}(\log Y^{2}-\log\sigma)]-\Tr(Y^{2})\log\Tr(Y^{2})\},\qquad\mathcal{E}(X)=\operatorname{Re}\langle X,\mathcal{L}X\rangle_{\sigma}.

Define the constants α2\alpha_{2} and α1\alpha_{1} as the best nonnegative constants in the L2L_{2}-logarithmic Sobolev inequality (LSI) and the modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality (MLSI), respectively:

(LSI) α2​Ent2,σ​(X)\displaystyle\alpha_{2}\Ent_{2,\sigma}(X) ≤ℰ⁡(X),\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{E}(X),
(MLSI) 2α1D(ρ∥σ)\displaystyle 2\alpha_{1}D(\rho\|\sigma) ≤ℐℒ​(ρ).\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{L}}(\rho).

By Gronwall’s lemma, MLSI is equivalent to exponential entropy decay from time zero [14, equations (5)–(6)]:

(3.3) D(Pt∗ρ∥σ)≤e−2​α1​tD(ρ∥σ),t≥0.D(P_{t*}\rho\|\sigma)\leq e^{-2\alpha_{1}t}D(\rho\|\sigma),\quad t\geq 0.

We also use the norm–entropy derivative [14, Theorem 4]:

(3.4) ∂rlog⁡‖X‖r,σ|r=2=Ent2,σ⁡(X)2​‖X‖2,σ2,X>0,\left.\partial_{r}\log\|X\|_{r,\sigma}\right|_{r=2}=\frac{\Ent_{2,\sigma}(X)}{2\|X\|_{2,\sigma}^{2}},\qquad X>0,

which gives αH≤α2\alpha_{H}\leq\alpha_{2} [14, Theorem 15(1)]. Direct Dirichlet-form comparison under KMS symmetry gives α1≥α2\alpha_{1}\geq\alpha_{2} under strong LpL_{p}-regularity [14, Propositions 8 and 13], a condition satisfied by GNS-symmetric semigroups but not known to follow from KMS symmetry. In summary, for a primitive KMS-symmetric semigroup

αH≤α2​≤(∗)​α1\alpha_{H}\leq\alpha_{2}\overset{(*)}{\leq}\alpha_{1}

where (*) requires strong LpL_{p}-regularity.

The next lemma shows that αH≤α2\alpha_{H}\leq\alpha_{2} and αH≤2​α1\alpha_{H}\leq 2\alpha_{1} without KMS symmetry or LpL_{p}-regularity. For KMS-symmetric semigroups, the argument from HC to MLSI was discussed in [12, Section 7, EQ. (7.2)–(7.3)].

Lemma 3.1 (Local HC curve).

Let r:[0,ε)→[2,∞)r:[0,\varepsilon)\to[2,\infty) be right differentiable at zero, with r⁡(0)=2r(0)=2 and r′​(0)=v>0r^{\prime}(0)=v>0. If ‖Ps‖2→r⁡(s)≤1\|P_{s}\|_{2\to r(s)}\leq 1 for 0≤s<ε0\leq s<\varepsilon, then

α1≥v4,α2≥v2,αH≥v4.\alpha_{1}\geq\frac{v}{4}\ ,\ \alpha_{2}\geq\frac{v}{2}\ ,\ \alpha_{H}\geq\frac{v}{4}\ .

In particular, we have αH≤2​α1\alpha_{H}\leq 2\alpha_{1} and αH≤α2\alpha_{H}\leq\alpha_{2}.

Proposition 2.2 gives

D(Ps∗ρ∥σ)≤2r⁡(s)D(ρ∥σ).D(P_{s*}\rho\|\sigma)\leq\frac{2}{r(s)}D(\rho\|\sigma).

Since 2/r⁡(s)=1−v​s/2+o⁡(s)2/r(s)=1-vs/2+o(s), differentiation at zero gives α1≥v/4\alpha_{1}\geq v/4. For the LSI constant, the norm–entropy derivative (3.4) gives

0≥dd​s​log⁡‖Ps​X‖r⁡(s),σ|s=0+=(v/2)​Ent2,σ⁡(X)−ℰ⁡(X)‖X‖2,σ2.0\geq\left.\frac{d}{ds}\log\|P_{s}X\|_{r(s),\sigma}\right|_{s=0^{+}}=\frac{(v/2)\Ent_{2,\sigma}(X)-\mathcal{E}(X)}{\|X\|_{2,\sigma}^{2}}.

Thus v​Ent2,σ⁡(X)≤2​ℰ​(X)v\Ent_{2,\sigma}(X)\leq 2\mathcal{E}(X), which gives α2≥v/2\alpha_{2}\geq v/2. For the all-time estimate, interpolation with ‖Ps‖∞→∞=1\|P_{s}\|_{\infty\to\infty}=1 gives

‖Ps‖p→p​r​(s)/2≤1,2≤p<∞.\|P_{s}\|_{p\to pr(s)/2}\leq 1,\qquad 2\leq p<\infty.

For fixed t>0t>0, composition over nn steps of length t/nt/n yields

‖Pt‖2→2​(r⁡(t/n)/2)n≤1,\|P_{t}\|_{2\to 2(r(t/n)/2)^{n}}\leq 1,

where the target exponent converges to 2​ev​t/22e^{vt/2} as n→∞n\to\infty. The bound on αH\alpha_{H} follows from 1+ev​t/2≤2​ev​t/21+e^{vt/2}\leq 2e^{vt/2} and norm monotonicity. ∎

3.2. Modified logarithmic Sobolev bounds

For a finite-dimensional primitive QMS Pt=e−ℒ​tP_{t}=e^{-\mathcal{L}t} with limt→∞Pt=Eσ\lim_{t\to\infty}P_{t}=E_{\sigma}, we define the KMS coercivity constant

λKMS:=inf0≠X∈ker⁡EσRe⁡⟨X,ℒ​X⟩σ‖X‖2,σ2≥0.\lambda_{\text{KMS}}:=\inf_{0\neq X\in\ker E_{\sigma}}\frac{\operatorname{Re}\langle X,\mathcal{L}X\rangle_{\sigma}}{\|X\|_{2,\sigma}^{2}}\geq 0.

Under KMS symmetry, ℒ\mathcal{L} is self-adjoint on L2​(σ)L_{2}(\sigma) and λK​M​S\lambda_{KMS} is exactly the spectral gap

(3.5) λKMS=inf0≠X∈ker⁡Eσ⟨X,ℒ​X⟩σ‖X‖2,σ2=min⁡(spec​(ℒ)∖{0})=:λ>0,\lambda_{\text{KMS}}=\inf_{0\neq X\in\ker E_{\sigma}}\frac{\langle X,\mathcal{L}X\rangle_{\sigma}}{\|X\|_{2,\sigma}^{2}}=\min(\text{spec}(\mathcal{L})\setminus\{0\})=:\lambda>0,

which is always positive in finite dimensions, and one has [14, Theorem 16]

(3.6) α1≤λ.\alpha_{1}\leq\lambda.

For a finite-dimensional QMS without KMS symmetry, one has α1≤2​λKMS\alpha_{1}\leq 2\lambda_{\text{KMS}}, with a factor of 22 lost through symmetrization.

We derive the modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality from hyperboundedness using the coercivity constant or spectral gap on centered elements. The argument applies with or without KMS symmetry and does not require LpL_{p}-regularity.

Theorem 3.2 (Bounds from centered coercivity).

Let (Pt)(P_{t}) be a σ\sigma-preserving primitive QMS with a positive KMS coercivity constant λK​M​S=λ>0\lambda_{KMS}=\lambda>0. Then

(3.7) α1≥αH2≥λ2+log⁡‖σ−1‖∞.\alpha_{1}\geq\frac{\alpha_{H}}{2}\geq\frac{\lambda}{2+\log\|\sigma^{-1}\|_{\infty}}.
Proof.

For X∈ker⁡EσX\in\ker E_{\sigma}, coercivity gives

dd​t​‖Pt​X‖2,σ2≤−2​λ​‖Pt​X‖2,σ2,\frac{d}{dt}\|P_{t}X\|_{2,\sigma}^{2}\leq-2\lambda\|P_{t}X\|_{2,\sigma}^{2},

which implies ‖Pt−Eσ‖2→2≤e−λ​t\|P_{t}-E_{\sigma}\|_{2\to 2}\leq e^{-\lambda t}. The elementary weighted norm comparison is

(3.8) ‖X‖r,σ≤‖σ−1‖∞1/2−1/r​‖X‖2,σ,2≤r<∞.\|X\|_{r,\sigma}\leq\|\sigma^{-1}\|_{\infty}^{1/2-1/r}\|X\|_{2,\sigma},\qquad 2\leq r<\infty.

Indeed, put Z=σ1/4​X​σ1/4Z=\sigma^{1/4}X\sigma^{1/4} and B=σ1/(2​r)−1/4B=\sigma^{1/(2r)-1/4}. The ideal property and Schatten norm monotonicity give

‖X‖r,σ=\displaystyle\|X\|_{r,\sigma}= ‖σ1/(2​r)−1/4​(σ1/4​X​σ1/4)​σ1/(2​r)−1/4‖r≤‖σ1/(2​r)−1/4‖∞2​‖σ1/4​X​σ1/4‖r\displaystyle\|\sigma^{1/(2r)-1/4}(\sigma^{1/4}X\sigma^{1/4})\sigma^{1/(2r)-1/4}\|_{r}\leq\|\sigma^{1/(2r)-1/4}\|_{\infty}^{2}\|\sigma^{1/4}X\sigma^{1/4}\|_{r}
≤\displaystyle\leq ‖σ−1‖∞1/2−1/r​‖σ1/4​X​σ1/4‖2=‖σ−1‖∞1/2−1/r​‖X‖2,σ\displaystyle\|\sigma^{-1}\|_{\infty}^{1/2-1/r}\|\sigma^{1/4}X\sigma^{1/4}\|_{2}=\|\sigma^{-1}\|_{\infty}^{1/2-1/r}\|X\|_{2,\sigma}

The case r=4r=4 is used in [22, Corollary 6]. Thus

‖Pt−Eσ‖2→r≤‖σ−1‖∞1/2−1/r​e−λ​t.\|P_{t}-E_{\sigma}\|_{2\to r}\leq\|\sigma^{-1}\|_{\infty}^{1/2-1/r}e^{-\lambda t}.

Lemma 2.3 and Proposition 2.2 give HC 2→r2\to r and EC with coefficient 2/r2/r whenever

(3.9) t≥log⁡(r−1)+(1−2/r)​log⁡‖σ−1‖∞2​λ.t\geq\frac{\log(r-1)+(1-2/r)\log\|\sigma^{-1}\|_{\infty}}{2\lambda}.

For r⁡(t)=1+e2​α​tr(t)=1+e^{2\alpha t}, this condition becomes

(3.10) (λ−α)​t≥log⁡‖σ−1‖∞2​tanh⁡(α​t).(\lambda-\alpha)t\geq\frac{\log\|\sigma^{-1}\|_{\infty}}{2}\tanh(\alpha t).

The elementary bound tanh⁡(α​t)≤α​t\tanh(\alpha t)\leq\alpha t shows that (3.10) holds for every t≥0t\geq 0 whenever

0≤α≤A:=2​λ2+log⁡‖σ−1‖∞.0\leq\alpha\leq A:=\frac{2\lambda}{2+\log\|\sigma^{-1}\|_{\infty}}.

In particular, choosing α=A\alpha=A gives

‖Pt‖2→1+e2​A​t,σ≤1(t≥0).\|P_{t}\|_{2\to 1+e^{2At},\sigma}\leq 1\qquad(t\geq 0).

By the definition of αH\alpha_{H} in (3.2), this implies αH≥A\alpha_{H}\geq A. Together with α1≥αH/2\alpha_{1}\geq\alpha_{H}/2 from Lemma 3.1, this proves (3.7). ∎

The above theorem gives HC and entropy decay using only coercivity and the smallest eigenvalue of σ\sigma, without KMS symmetry or LpL_{p}-regularity. A similar estimate for the LSI constant α2\alpha_{2} was obtained in [22] for KMS-symmetric semigroups through Rothaus’s lemma. Using this estimate to bound the MLSI constant α1\alpha_{1} would require LpL_{p}-regularity. In particular, our bound (3.7) improves the qualitative MLSI conclusion for primitive KMS-symmetric semigroups that also appears in [27, Theorem 3.1] and [28, Corollary 6.1]. Moreover, the logarithmic loss log⁡‖σ−1‖∞\log\|\sigma^{-1}\|_{\infty} is asymptotically tight, as in the classical case.

A faster curve is available after a delay: for 0<α<λ0<\alpha<\lambda, use tanh⁡(α​t)≤1\tanh(\alpha t)\leq 1 in (3.10) to similarly obtain the HC and EC estimates whenever

(3.11) t≥log⁡‖σ−1‖∞2​(λ−α).t\geq\frac{\log\|\sigma^{-1}\|_{\infty}}{2(\lambda-\alpha)}.

For the tracial state σ=I/d\sigma=I/d on MdM_{d}, a stronger reversible comparison is recalled in [17, Theorem 2.2]:

α1≥α2≥2​(1−2/d)​λlog⁡(d−1),\alpha_{1}\geq\alpha_{2}\geq\frac{2(1-2/d)\lambda}{\log(d-1)},

with coefficient 11 at d=2d=2. Thus (3.7) is a general faithful-state bound, not an optimal tracial bound.

The norm comparison at time zero t=0t=0 can be replaced by a single HB estimate. The interpolation argument below follows [22, Theorem 5] and the classical argument of [9, Theorem 3.9]. Combining it with the centered HC criterion gives the following bounds.

Theorem 3.3 (MLSI from a hyperbounded estimate).

Let PtP_{t} be a primitive QMS that is KMS-symmetric with respect to σ\sigma, and let λ>0\lambda>0 be its spectral gap. Assume that for some 2<q≤∞2<q\leq\infty, tq>0t_{q}>0, and Mq≥1M_{q}\geq 1,

(3.12) ‖Ptq‖2→q≤Mq.\|P_{t_{q}}\|_{2\to q}\leq M_{q}.

Then

(3.13) α1≥β:=(1−2/q)​λ2​[λ​tq+log⁡Mq+1−2/q].\alpha_{1}\geq\beta:=\frac{(1-2/q)\lambda}{2[\lambda t_{q}+\log M_{q}+1-2/q]}.

Moreover, the LSI and HC constants satisfy

(3.14) α2≥2​β,αH≥β.\alpha_{2}\geq 2\beta,\qquad\alpha_{H}\geq\beta.
Proof.

Set bq=1−2/qb_{q}=1-2/q. We use the Stein–Weiss argument of [22, equations (18)–(19)]. For Kz=e−z​tq​ℒK_{z}=e^{-zt_{q}\mathcal{L}} on the strip 0≤Re⁡z≤10\leq\operatorname{Re}z\leq 1, KMS self-adjointness gives ‖Ki​y‖2→2=1\|K_{iy}\|_{2\to 2}=1 and ‖K1+i​y‖2→q≤Mq\|K_{1+iy}\|_{2\to q}\leq M_{q}. (3.15) ‖Pu‖2→p⁡(u)≤Mqu/tq,p⁡(u)=21−bq​u/tq,0≤u≤tq.\|P_{u}\|_{2\to p(u)}\leq M_{q}^{u/t_{q}},\qquad p(u)=\frac{2}{1-b_{q}u/t_{q}},\qquad 0\leq u\leq t_{q}.

For 2≤r≤q2\leq r\leq q with r<∞r<\infty, put

(3.16) θr=1−2/rbq,ur=tq​θr.\theta_{r}=\frac{1-2/r}{b_{q}},\qquad u_{r}=t_{q}\theta_{r}.

Since ‖PT|ker⁡Eσ‖2→r≤Mqθr​e−λ⁡(T−ur)\|P_{T}|_{\ker E_{\sigma}}\|_{2\to r}\leq M_{q}^{\theta_{r}}e^{-\lambda(T-u_{r})} for T≥urT\geq u_{r}, Lemma 2.3 gives HC as soon as

(3.17) T≥F⁡(r):=tq​θr+θr​log⁡Mq+12​log⁡(r−1)λ.T\geq F(r):=t_{q}\theta_{r}+\frac{\theta_{r}\log M_{q}+\frac{1}{2}\log(r-1)}{\lambda}.

Together with Proposition 2.2, this proves the finite-exponent estimates

(3.18) ∥PT∥2→r≤1,D(PT∗ρ∥σ)≤2rD(ρ∥σ).\|P_{T}\|_{2\to r}\leq 1,\qquad D(P_{T*}\rho\|\sigma)\leq\frac{2}{r}D(\rho\|\sigma).

The function FF is continuously differentiable and strictly increasing on [2,q)[2,q), with F⁡(2)=0F(2)=0 and

F′​(2)=λ​tq+log⁡Mq+bq2​bq​λ.F^{\prime}(2)=\frac{\lambda t_{q}+\log M_{q}+b_{q}}{2b_{q}\lambda}.

Its inverse r​(T)=F−1​(T)r(T)=F^{-1}(T) is a local HC curve, defined for T≥0T\geq 0 sufficiently small, whose initial slope is r′​(0)=4​βr^{\prime}(0)=4\beta. Lemma 3.1 proves all three bounds. ∎

The MLSI and LS2 estimates use the initial slope directly; the extension to a full HC curve gives the rate β\beta. In the normalization of [22], Theorems 3.2 and 3.3 give α2≥2​λ/(2+log⁡‖σ−1‖∞)\alpha_{2}\geq 2\lambda/(2+\log\|\sigma^{-1}\|_{\infty}) and α2≥2​β\alpha_{2}\geq 2\beta, respectively. These are twice the corresponding bounds in [22, Eqs. (30), (11)], after reversing the generator sign. The interpolation method and the existence of an all-time HC curve without LpL_{p}-regularity are already present in [22].

3.3. Delayed hypercontractivity and the lack of MLSI

Theorems 3.2 and 3.3 use L2L_{2}-decay of centered elements with prefactor one. In finite dimensions, primitivity instead only guarantees an estimate

(3.19) ‖Pt−Eσ‖2→2≤C​e−ν​t,t≥0,\|P_{t}-E_{\sigma}\|_{2\to 2}\leq Ce^{-\nu t},\qquad t\geq 0,

for some C≥1C\geq 1 and ν>0\nu>0. Indeed, every positive rate below the smallest real part of the spectrum of ℒ|K\mathcal{L}|_{K} is admissible after absorbing the Jordan polynomial factors into CC. This does not ensure C=1C=1, and hence does not give the coercivity required in Theorem 3.2.

The norm comparison (3.8) gives

‖Pt−Eσ‖2→r≤C​‖σ−1‖∞1/2−1/r​e−ν​t,2≤r<∞.\|P_{t}-E_{\sigma}\|_{2\to r}\leq C\|\sigma^{-1}\|_{\infty}^{1/2-1/r}e^{-\nu t},\qquad 2\leq r<\infty.

For r⁡(t)=1+e2​α​tr(t)=1+e^{2\alpha t}, Lemma 2.3 gives HC whenever

(ν−α)​t≥log⁡C+12​log⁡‖σ−1‖∞​tanh⁡(α​t).(\nu-\alpha)t\geq\log C+\frac{1}{2}\log\|\sigma^{-1}\|_{\infty}\tanh(\alpha t).

Since tanh⁡(α​t)≤1\tanh(\alpha t)\leq 1, for every 0<α<ν0<\alpha<\nu and

(3.20) t≥τ⁡(α):=log⁡C+12​log⁡‖σ−1‖∞ν−α,t\geq\tau(\alpha):=\frac{\log C+\frac{1}{2}\log\|\sigma^{-1}\|_{\infty}}{\nu-\alpha},

we have

(3.21) ∥Pt∥2→1+e2​α​t≤1,D(Pt∗ρ∥σ)≤21+e2​α​tD(ρ∥σ)≤e−α​tD(ρ∥σ).\|P_{t}\|_{2\to 1+e^{2\alpha t}}\leq 1,\quad D(P_{t*}\rho\|\sigma)\leq\frac{2}{1+e^{2\alpha t}}D(\rho\|\sigma)\leq e^{-\alpha t}D(\rho\|\sigma).

Here the entropy estimate follows from Proposition 2.2 and 2/(1+e2​α​t)=e−α​t/cosh⁡(α​t)2/(1+e^{2\alpha t})=e^{-\alpha t}/\cosh(\alpha t). Nevertheless, such a delayed estimate does not imply a positive MLSI constant α1>0\alpha_{1}>0: it does not provide entropy decay from time zero.

The following qubit model makes this limitation explicit. It appears in [10, section “Hypocoercivity and Physical Intuition”]; the same generator and zero-entropy-production states occur in [27, Propositions 4.1–4.2].

Example 3.4 (Delayed decay with zero MLSI constant).

Let σ=I/2\sigma=I/2 on M2M_{2} and h,γ>0h,\gamma>0. The QMS with generator

−ℒ∗​(ρ)=−i⁡[h​σx,ρ]+γ⁡(σz​ρ​σz−ρ)-\mathcal{L}_{*}(\rho)=-i[h\sigma_{x},\rho]+\gamma(\sigma_{z}\rho\sigma_{z}-\rho)

is primitive and satisfies (3.19) for suitable C,νC,\nu, and therefore obeys the delayed HC and EC estimates (3.21), but α1=0\alpha_{1}=0 and λKMS=0\lambda_{\mathrm{KMS}}=0.

To verify these assertions, write ρ=(I+x​σx+y​σy+z​σz)/2\rho=(I+x\sigma_{x}+y\sigma_{y}+z\sigma_{z})/2. The Bloch equations are

x˙=−2​γ​x,dd​t​(yz)=(−2​γ−2​h2​h0)​(yz).\dot{x}=-2\gamma x,\qquad\frac{d}{dt}\begin{pmatrix}y\\ z\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\gamma&-2h\\ 2h&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}y\\ z\end{pmatrix}.

The two eigenvalues of the displayed matrix are −γ±γ2−4​h2-\gamma\pm\sqrt{\gamma^{2}-4h^{2}} and have strictly negative real parts, so every state converges to I/2I/2. For every 0<ν<γ−Re⁡γ2−4​h20<\nu<\gamma-\operatorname{Re}\sqrt{\gamma^{2}-4h^{2}}, matrix exponential estimates give a finite C≥1C\geq 1 in (3.19), including the possible Jordan case.

For ρa=(I+a​σz)/2\rho_{a}=(I+a\sigma_{z})/2, 0<|a|<10<|a|<1, the dissipative part vanishes and the Hamiltonian part has zero entropy production. Hence

ℐℒ(ρa)=0,D(ρa∥I/2)>0,\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{L}}(\rho_{a})=0,\qquad D(\rho_{a}\|I/2)>0,

which gives α1=0\alpha_{1}=0. Finally, Re⁡⟨σz,ℒ​σz⟩σ=0\operatorname{Re}\langle\sigma_{z},\mathcal{L}\sigma_{z}\rangle_{\sigma}=0 and L2L_{2} contractivity imply λKMS=0\lambda_{\mathrm{KMS}}=0.

4. Entropy contraction and approximate tensorization

For two conditional expectations, approximate tensorization easily implies entropy contraction of their average. Theorem 4.1 proves that the converse also holds up to an absolute constant. The proof controls the Jensen–Shannon term in the entropy loss.

Let Ei:B⁡(ℋ)→𝒩iE_{i}:B(\mathcal{H})\to\mathcal{N}_{i}, i=1,2i=1,2, be conditional expectations preserving a common faithful state σ\sigma. Namely, each EiE_{i} is a unital completely positive map satisfying

Ei(AXB)=AEi(X)B∀A,B∈𝒩i and Ei∗σ=σ.E_{i}(AXB)=AE_{i}(X)B\ \ \forall\ \ A,B\in\mathcal{N}_{i}\ \text{ and }\qquad E_{i*}\sigma=\sigma\ .

Each expectation is uniquely determined by the state σ\sigma it preserves and its range 𝒩i\mathcal{N}_{i}, and acts as an orthogonal projection in L2​(σ)L_{2}(\sigma) [4, Definition 1 and Proposition 1]. The intersection range 𝒩=𝒩1∩𝒩2\mathcal{N}=\mathcal{N}_{1}\cap\mathcal{N}_{2} also admits a σ\sigma-preserving expectation E𝒩E_{\mathcal{N}}. In this section, we focus on the average of the two conditional expectations

Φav=E1+E22\Phi_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{E_{1}+E_{2}}{2}

as a positive self-adjoint contraction with fixed space 𝒩\mathcal{N}. Its powers Φavn\Phi_{\mathrm{av}}^{n} converge to E𝒩E_{\mathcal{N}}.

For a state ρ\rho, write

(4.1) ρi=Ei∗ρ,ρ𝒩=E𝒩∗ρ,D𝒩(ρ)=D(ρ∥ρ𝒩).\rho_{i}=E_{i*}\rho,\qquad\rho_{\mathcal{N}}=E_{\mathcal{N}*}\rho,\qquad D_{\mathcal{N}}(\rho)=D(\rho\|\rho_{\mathcal{N}}).

The inclusion 𝒩⊂𝒩i\mathcal{N}\subset\mathcal{N}_{i} and the chain rule imply that

(4.2) E𝒩Ei=E𝒩=EiE𝒩,D(ρ||ρ𝒩)=D(ρ∥ρi)+D(ρi||ρ𝒩),i=1,2,E_{\mathcal{N}}E_{i}=E_{\mathcal{N}}=E_{i}E_{\mathcal{N}},\qquad D(\rho||\rho_{\mathcal{N}})=D(\rho\|\rho_{i})+D(\rho_{i}||\rho_{\mathcal{N}}),\qquad i=1,2,

for all states ρ\rho, including singular states [13, Lemma 3.4 of the arXiv version]. It is known that the exact entropy tensorization inequality (also called entropy factorization)

D(ρ∥ρ𝒩)≤D(ρ∥ρ1)+D(ρ∥ρ2)D(\rho\|\rho_{\mathcal{N}})\leq D(\rho\|\rho_{1})+D(\rho\|\rho_{2})

holds for every state ρ\rho if and only if the conditional expectations satisfy the commuting square condition

E1​E2=E2​E1=E𝒩.E_{1}E_{2}=E_{2}E_{1}=E_{\mathcal{N}}.

We use the defect-free approximate tensorization inequality of [4, Definition 2, with defect d=0d=0], but allow any constant c>0c>0 rather than imposing c≥1c\geq 1. We say that (E1,E2)(E_{1},E_{2}) satisfies approximate tensorization with constant c>0c>0, denoted by AT⁡(c)\mathrm{AT}(c), if

(4.3) D(ρ||ρ𝒩)≤c(D(ρ∥ρ1)+D(ρ∥ρ2))for every state ρ.D(\rho||\rho_{\mathcal{N}})\leq c\bigl(D(\rho\|\rho_{1})+D(\rho\|\rho_{2})\bigr)\qquad\text{for every state $\rho$}.

The optimal coefficient cATc_{\mathrm{AT}} is the infimum of all admissible constants c>0c>0, with cAT=+∞c_{\mathrm{AT}}=+\infty if none exists. Thus cATc_{\mathrm{AT}} is the sharp coefficient in (4.3) and may be smaller than one. For example, if E1=E2=E𝒩≠idE_{1}=E_{2}=E_{\mathcal{N}}\neq\id, then cAT=1/2c_{\mathrm{AT}}=1/2. If 𝒩=B⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{N}=B(\mathcal{H}), both expectations are the identity and cAT=0c_{\mathrm{AT}}=0; the formulas below involving entropy ratios or 1/cAT1/c_{\mathrm{AT}} are used only when 𝒩≠B⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{N}\neq B(\mathcal{H}).

The averaged map is

(4.4) Φav=E1+E22,Φav,∗​ρ=ρ1+ρ22,\Phi_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{E_{1}+E_{2}}{2},\qquad\Phi_{\mathrm{av},*}\rho=\frac{\rho_{1}+\rho_{2}}{2},

Entropy contraction for the average means

(4.5) D(Φav,∗ρ||ρ𝒩)≤ηD(ρ||ρ𝒩)for every state ρ,0≤η<1,D(\Phi_{\mathrm{av},*}\rho||\rho_{\mathcal{N}})\leq\eta D(\rho||\rho_{\mathcal{N}})\qquad\text{for every state $\rho$},\qquad 0\leq\eta<1,

and is denoted by EC𝒩​(η)\mathrm{EC}_{\mathcal{N}}(\eta). The reference state on both sides is ρ𝒩\rho_{\mathcal{N}}, which depends on the input ρ\rho.

The known implication from AT to average EC follows from (4.2) and convexity [8, Eqs. (11)–(12)]:

(4.6) D(Φav,∗ρ||ρ𝒩)≤12∑i=12D(ρi∥ρ𝒩)≤(1−12​cA​T)D(ρ∥ρ𝒩).D(\Phi_{\mathrm{av},*}\rho||\rho_{\mathcal{N}})\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{2}D(\rho_{i}\|\rho_{\mathcal{N}})\leq\left(1-\frac{1}{2c_{AT}}\right)D(\rho\|\rho_{\mathcal{N}}).

The converse requires an upper bound on the entropy lost in the averaging step.

Theorem 4.1 (AT from EC).

Let Ei:B⁡(ℋ)→𝒩iE_{i}:B(\mathcal{H})\to\mathcal{N}_{i}, i=1,2i=1,2, be conditional expectations preserving a common faithful state σ\sigma, and let E𝒩E_{\mathcal{N}} be the σ\sigma-preserving conditional expectation onto the intersection 𝒩=𝒩1∩𝒩2\mathcal{N}=\mathcal{N}_{1}\cap\mathcal{N}_{2}. Assume that the averaged map satisfies the following entropy contraction inequality for some 0<η<10<\eta<1 and all states ρ\rho:

(4.7) D(Φav,∗ρ||ρ𝒩)≤ηD(ρ||ρ𝒩).\displaystyle D(\Phi_{\mathrm{av},*}\rho||\rho_{\mathcal{N}})\leq\eta D(\rho||\rho_{\mathcal{N}}).

Then the following AT inequality holds:

(4.8) D(ρ||ρ𝒩)≤32​(1−η)(D(ρ∥ρ1)+D(ρ∥ρ2))for every state ρ.D(\rho||\rho_{\mathcal{N}})\leq\frac{3}{2(1-\eta)}\left(D(\rho\|\rho_{1})+D(\rho\|\rho_{2})\right)\qquad\text{for every state $\rho$}.

In particular,

(4.9) cAT≤32​(1−η).c_{\mathrm{AT}}\leq\frac{3}{2(1-\eta)}.
Proof.

Set ρ¯=(ρ1+ρ2)/2\bar{\rho}=(\rho_{1}+\rho_{2})/2. For states A,BA,B, recall the quantum Jensen–Shannon divergence [24, Section 1.2]

(4.10) J⁡(A,B)=12​D​(A∥A+B2)+12​D​(B∥A+B2).J(A,B)=\frac{1}{2}D\left(A\,\middle\|\,\frac{A+B}{2}\right)+\frac{1}{2}D\left(B\,\middle\|\,\frac{A+B}{2}\right).

Donald’s identity [21, equation (5)] reads

(4.11) 12D(A∥R)+12D(B∥R)=D(A+B2∥R)+J(A,B),\frac{1}{2}D(A\|R)+\frac{1}{2}D(B\|R)=D\left(\frac{A+B}{2}\,\middle\|\,R\right)+J(A,B),

when supp⁡A,supp⁡B⊆supp⁡R\supp A,\supp B\subseteq\supp R. Taking A=ρ1A=\rho_{1}, B=ρ2B=\rho_{2}, and R=ρ𝒩R=\rho_{\mathcal{N}}, and using (4.2) gives the entropy-loss identity

(4.12) D(ρ∥ρ𝒩)−D(ρ¯∥ρ𝒩)=12(D(ρ∥ρ1)+D(ρ∥ρ2))+J(ρ1,ρ2).D(\rho\|\rho_{\mathcal{N}})-D(\bar{\rho}\|\rho_{\mathcal{N}})=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(D(\rho\|\rho_{1})+D(\rho\|\rho_{2})\bigr)+J(\rho_{1},\rho_{2}).

By Virosztek’s metric theorem [24, Theorem 1], for all states A,B,CA,B,C,

(4.13) J⁡(A,C)≤J⁡(A,B)+J⁡(B,C).\sqrt{J(A,C)}\leq\sqrt{J(A,B)}+\sqrt{J(B,C)}.

Taking R=BR=B in (4.11) and using the nonnegativity of relative entropy, we also have

(4.14) J(A,B)≤12D(A∥B),J(A,B)≤12D(B∥A).J(A,B)\leq\frac{1}{2}D(A\|B),\qquad J(A,B)\leq\frac{1}{2}D(B\|A).

Using the original input ρ\rho as the intermediate state in (4.13) yields

J⁡(ρ1,ρ2)≤J⁡(ρ1,ρ)+J⁡(ρ,ρ2)≤D(ρ∥ρ1)2+D(ρ∥ρ2)2.\displaystyle\sqrt{J(\rho_{1},\rho_{2})}\leq\sqrt{J(\rho_{1},\rho)}+\sqrt{J(\rho,\rho_{2})}\leq\sqrt{\frac{D(\rho\|\rho_{1})}{2}}+\sqrt{\frac{D(\rho\|\rho_{2})}{2}}.

Combining the above estimates with the entropy contraction assumption (4.7), we obtain

(4.15) (1−η)D(ρ||ρ𝒩)\displaystyle(1-\eta)D(\rho||\rho_{\mathcal{N}}) ≤D(ρ||ρ𝒩)−D(ρ¯||ρ𝒩)\displaystyle\leq D(\rho||\rho_{\mathcal{N}})-D(\bar{\rho}||\rho_{\mathcal{N}})
(4.16) ≤12(D(ρ∥ρ1)+D(ρ∥ρ2))+J(ρ1,ρ2)\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\left(D(\rho\|\rho_{1})+D(\rho\|\rho_{2})\right)+J(\rho_{1},\rho_{2})
(4.17) ≤12(D(ρ∥ρ1)+D(ρ∥ρ2))+12(D(ρ∥ρ1)+D(ρ∥ρ2))2\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\left(D(\rho\|\rho_{1})+D(\rho\|\rho_{2})\right)+\frac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{D(\rho\|\rho_{1})}+\sqrt{D(\rho\|\rho_{2})}\right)^{2}
(4.18) =D(ρ∥ρ1)+D(ρ∥ρ2)+D(ρ∥ρ1)D(ρ∥ρ2)\displaystyle=D(\rho\|\rho_{1})+D(\rho\|\rho_{2})+\sqrt{D(\rho\|\rho_{1})D(\rho\|\rho_{2})}
(4.19) ≤32(D(ρ∥ρ1)+D(ρ∥ρ2)),\displaystyle\leq\frac{3}{2}\bigl(D(\rho\|\rho_{1})+D(\rho\|\rho_{2})\bigr),

where the first inequality follows from entropy contraction D(ρ¯||ρ𝒩)≤ηD(ρ||ρ𝒩)D(\bar{\rho}||\rho_{\mathcal{N}})\leq\eta D(\rho||\rho_{\mathcal{N}}). This completes the proof. ∎

The above bound holds for an arbitrary intersection 𝒩1∩𝒩2=𝒩\mathcal{N}_{1}\cap\mathcal{N}_{2}=\mathcal{N}. It also holds completely: a complete EC bound with one coefficient η<1\eta<1 implies complete AT with the same constant 3/[2​(1−η)]3/[2(1-\eta)]. Approximate tensorization for noncommuting expectations and its complete versions are studied in [4, 11]. Gao and Rouzé [11, Corollary 5.4 and Remark 5.5] also obtain index-independent bounds from mixing in completely positive order; converting L2L_{2} estimates into that mixing condition introduces a conditional-expectation index. Theorem 4.1 instead starts with an entropy contraction coefficient. Its conversion to AT has no additional dimension or index factor.

For 𝒩≠B⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{N}\neq B(\mathcal{H}), the optimal entropy contraction coefficient and the optimal AT coefficient are given by

(4.20) ηav\displaystyle\eta_{\mathrm{av}} =supρ≠ρ𝒩D(Φav,∗ρ||ρ𝒩)D(ρ||ρ𝒩),\displaystyle=\sup_{\rho\neq\rho_{\mathcal{N}}}\frac{D(\Phi_{\mathrm{av},*}\rho||\rho_{\mathcal{N}})}{D(\rho||\rho_{\mathcal{N}})},
cA​T\displaystyle c_{AT} =supρ≠ρ𝒩D(ρ||ρ𝒩)D(ρ∥ρ1)+D(ρ∥ρ2).\displaystyle=\sup_{\rho\neq\rho_{\mathcal{N}}}\frac{D(\rho||\rho_{\mathcal{N}})}{D(\rho\|\rho_{1})+D(\rho\|\rho_{2})}.

The denominator defining cA​Tc_{AT} is positive for ρ≠ρ𝒩\rho\neq\rho_{\mathcal{N}}: if both defects vanish, both state expectations fix ρ\rho, and convergence of the averaged powers gives ρ=ρ𝒩\rho=\rho_{\mathcal{N}}. Moreover, (4.2) shows that each defect is at most D𝒩​(ρ)D_{\mathcal{N}}(\rho), so cA​T≥1/2c_{AT}\geq 1/2. The above discussion shows that

12​cA​T≤1−ηav≤32​cA​T.\frac{1}{2c_{AT}}\leq 1-\eta_{\mathrm{av}}\leq\frac{3}{2c_{AT}}.

Here we use the convention 1/(+∞)=01/(+\infty)=0. We can now derive AT from HC for the averaged map.

Corollary 4.2 (HC implies AT).

Let Ei:B⁡(ℋ)→𝒩iE_{i}:B(\mathcal{H})\to\mathcal{N}_{i}, i=1,2i=1,2, be two σ\sigma-preserving conditional expectations with trivial intersection 𝒩1∩𝒩2=ℂ​1\mathcal{N}_{1}\cap\mathcal{N}_{2}=\mathbb{C}1. Suppose that, for some 1<p<q<∞1<p<q<\infty,

‖Φav‖p→q,σ≤1.\|\Phi_{\mathrm{av}}\|_{p\to q,\sigma}\leq 1.

Then we have

D(Φav,∗ρ||σ)≤min{pq,q′p′}D(ρ||σ),D(\Phi_{\mathrm{av},*}\rho||\sigma)\leq\min\{\frac{p}{q},\frac{q^{\prime}}{p^{\prime}}\}D(\rho||\sigma),

where p′=p/(p−1)p^{\prime}=p/(p-1) and q′=q/(q−1)q^{\prime}=q/(q-1). This further implies

(4.21) cAT≤32​(1−min⁡{pq,q′p′}).c_{\mathrm{AT}}\leq\frac{3}{2\bigl(1-\min\{\frac{p}{q},\frac{q^{\prime}}{p^{\prime}}\}\bigr)}.

Here we use the fact that the average Φav\Phi_{\mathrm{av}} is KMS self-adjoint. For each fixed system with scalar intersection, this implies ‖Φav−Eσ‖2→2<1\|\Phi_{\mathrm{av}}-E_{\sigma}\|_{2\to 2}<1. Together with any finite 2→q2\to q endpoint, Theorem 2.4 also supplies an HC exponent and hence a finite AT constant.
